summary:
Bursa stands under the national framework of Türkiye, where hostility toward trans people has been formalised as state policy rather than left to residual prejudice. The Kaos GL LGBTI+ Human Rights Report 2025 recorded 313 violations in a single year, roughly two and a half times the 2024 total, with 299 detention decisions, 256 recorded through formal channels and 43 taken off the record.

Kaos GL's launch of the report "A major siege against LGBTI+ people in 2025: Hostility turned into state policy" documents hostility institutionalised as explicit state policy. Senior officials' hate speech and instructions issued to public institutions under a Year of the Family banner created a climate that encouraged human-rights violations, and regulatory and supervisory bodies systematically restricted freedom of expression and artistic freedom. The findings were presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen.

Human Rights Watch identifies the government's stated position of protecting "the family" and "public morals" as the rhetorical basis for legitimising stigma of LGBT people, language under which a draft legislative package effectively criminalising LGBT people was before the government as of October 2025.

The leaked 11th Judicial Package, reported by Human Rights Watch on 29 October 2025, would amend the Turkish penal and civil codes to criminalise behaviour deemed "contrary to biological sex and general morality" and would punish taking part in a same-sex engagement or marriage ceremony with up to four years in prison. The draft would also raise the minimum age for gender-affirming health care including surgery from 18 to 25, require permanent infertility as a condition, and punish health professionals who perform such care. Human Rights Watch calls it one of the most alarming rollbacks of LGBT rights in decades; 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association oppose the draft. It had not been passed when reported, yet authorities have acted as though the prohibitions were already in force.

Street-level enforcement in Istanbul illustrates that point. In 2025 Istanbul police stopped roughly 20 trans women on the street, in shops and in cafés in the Beyoğlu district and held them at the Taksim Şehit Haşim Usta Police Station for "General Information Gathering" background checks before release. Legal experts cited in the reporting argue that such checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights. One of the women detained stated that the police took no fines but documented them anyway, adding that the new law had not yet been passed even as enforcement was already being applied to them.

Turkey requires foreign nationals to carry original photo identification at transit checkpoints, including in holiday destinations, with fines of up to 3,000 Turkish lira for non-compliance and formal warnings of detention. Foreign visitors stopped at these checkpoints must produce original documents, creating a direct outing risk whenever appearance and passport gender marker do not match; every checkpoint interaction is an occasion on which documents can be compared against presentation.

Violence against trans people in Türkiye is lethal and the state response is markedly asymmetric. Six deaths were linked to anti-LGBTQ violence in 2025, three of which rights organisations classified as hate killings, and transgender individuals were disproportionately affected. In August 2024 the trans woman Yaşam was knifed in Bakırköy, Istanbul by a 17-year-old attacker; the perpetrator was released while the victim was herself referred for arrest, a detention asymmetry activists treat as evidence of a state policy of hate.

Transition-related care is tightening. A Health Ministry regulation reported in September 2025, following a Kayseri Provincial Health Directorate circular that added "gender reassignment" as an official reason for medical-board reports, barred hospitals from recording the "other" option and required e-reports to be issued. The change risks profiling trans patients in official records and restricting access to transition care, including for a visitor presenting at a Turkish hospital.
tangentialFactors:
Monitoring of the 2025 Istanbul Trans and LGBTI+ Pride Week by the Truth Justice Memory Center found that violations of international human-rights law continuing since 2015 persisted through 2025, with senior officials' discriminatory rhetoric deepening homophobia and transphobia and entrenching discrimination against LGBT people and their allies. Pride events remain flashpoints, and the pattern of official rhetoric driving street-level hostility applies to Bursa's own public events.

Prison conditions for LGBT detainees are governed by segregation and isolation rather than gender-matched placement. The Prison Insider country profile on Türkiye, prepared with the Civil Society in the Penal System Association and using ILGA World data, documents arbitrary body and strip searches, de facto solitary confinement with restricted access to healthcare, and refusals of hospital transfer out of fear of other male prisoners. There is no policy or staff training to identify the needs of LGBT prisoners, administration operates on a binary, heteronormative basis, transfers frequently disrupt visits and solidarity networks, and complaints are ineffective and can attract further violence. A foreign visitor detained in Bursa would enter the same machinery.

The underlying pattern is longstanding. Human Rights Watch's 2008 report We Need a Law for Liberation, drawn from more than 70 interviews over three years, documented continuing beatings, robberries and abuse against gay men and transgender people. That report predates the legal changes made after 2018 and is cited as historical evidence of the regime's depth rather than as a statement of current law.
localsOnly:
Trans prisoners are held by registered sex in gendered facilities. A transgender prisoner identified as Poyraz was found dead in a cell at Sincan Women's Prison near Ankara on 1 December 2025. Rights groups coordinated from Human Rights Association branches in Istanbul, Ankara, İzmir, Diyarbakır, Mersin and Aydın demanded an independent investigation, and accounts from other trans prisoners and visiting lawyers reported that four transgender inmates had been sent for psychiatric evaluation shortly before the death, that medical staff arrived only after a prolonged delay, that prosecutors and crime-scene investigators entered the prison two days later, and that witness statements were not taken.

The case was raised in parliament by opposition MP Sevda Karaca on 12 December 2025, confirming that Türkiye places trans prisoners according to their registered sex, with a trans man held in a women's prison, and that custody conditions for trans prisoners were under formal contestation at state level by the end of 2025.

Domestic opposition to the draft judicial package is organised rather than absent: 15 Turkish LGBT groups and the Turkish Medical Association are on record against it, and Kaos GL's monitoring work is carried out publicly, with its 2025 findings presented by lawyer Kerem Dikmen at a documented launch event.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Bursa-specific incident, enforcement action or monitoring figure is sourced in this record. The findings are national in scope or drawn from Istanbul and Ankara, and are applied to Bursa as the framework a visitor there would stand under; local policing practice in Bursa itself is unresolved.

Whether the 11th Judicial Package has been enacted is unresolved. It was reported as a leaked draft on 29 October 2025 with no source confirming passage, and no source confirms whether enforcement predating enactment has a formal legal basis.

The claim that GBT-style checks violate Article 5 of the European Convention on Human Rights is attributed to legal experts cited in reporting; no ruling or finding against the practice is sourced here.

The scope and enforcement of the September 2025 Health Ministry regulation, and whether it applies uniformly to every hospital a visitor might attend, are not sourced beyond the Kayseri circular described. Online framing of the change as an "LGBT opening" is contested and unresolved.

The Kaos GL violation and detention counts rest on that organisation's own monitoring methodology, which is not detailed in this record. The 2025 tally of six deaths linked to anti-LGBTQ violence and three classified hate killings is not attributed to a named source in the inventory.
